newsitem.title: UK: British women find work quicker than men - survey.
newsitem.headline: British women find work quicker than men - survey.

text.p: British women who find themselves out of work get a job more quickly than their male counterparts, the Office for National Statistics said on Thursday.
The ONS spring Labour Force Survey showed 34 percent of all unemployed women had been out of work for less than three months compared with just 22 percent of men.
Of the long-term unemployed, 28 percent of all jobless women had been out of work for a year or more while 45 percent of unemployed men had not worked in the last 12 months.
The ONS uses the International Labour Organisation's definition of unemployment for the purposes of its survey.

That includes those who were without a job at the time the survey was conducted, were available to start work in the next fortnight, had actively looked for work in the last four weeks or had found a job and were waiting to start.

Not only do women find work quicker, fewer find themselves in the jobless queues, the survey showed. In March, the ILO unemployment rate was 6.5 percent for British women of working age while the equivalent for men was 9.7 percent.

The ILO rate differs from the British government's definition. The newly-introduced jobseekers allowance, which replaced old-style unemployment benefit last year, makes more demands on claimants in terms of actively looking for work.
Due to a backlog of claims caused by the changes, falls in British unemployment have been overstated by official figures over the past few months.

After a staggering 95,800 fall in unemployment in November, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said sweeping change to the benefits system including the JSA accounted for some of the drop but said around 50,000 of the fall was genuine.
In January, the jobs queues were cut by a further 67,800 taking the overall unemployment rate down to 6.5 percent -- a six-year low -- according to official British figures.
Those figures list 1.9 million people as jobless. The ILO figure for the autumn period last year was 2.23 million.
Although women get back into work faster on average, the survey was not all good news as far as they were concerned.

It showed that although the number of women in managerial and professional jobs has increased, they still only represent 32 percent of managers and administrators, 35 percent of health professionals and 29 percent of buyers, brokers and sales representatives.
The so-called glass ceiling which is alleged to stop women reaching the higher rungs of the corporate ladder appears to be intact to some extent.
Some 85 percent of women are employed in service industries, the survey showed, in many cases in part-time or low paid jobs.
There were 1.3 million more women in employment in spring 1996 than 10 years previously but almost 700,000 of those jobs were part-time, it said.
Average hourly earnings of women full-time employees of working age at seven pounds were well below that for men, who earned eight pounds.
